faq.a: Dysmetria is a type of ataxia that specifically refers to inaccurate movement distance; ataxia includes gait instability and broader coordination loss.
faq.q: Is dysmetria the same as ataxia?

faq.a: Yes, if caused by an acute, treatable condition such as infection, stroke, or toxin exposure; chronic degenerative causes are less likely to improve.
MRI detects early ischemia, small tumours, and demyelination that CT may miss, providing a definitive diagnosis when available.
faq.q: Why is MRI preferred over CT?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden dysmetria and vomiting – what is your immediate diagnostic step and why? — Obtain non‑contrast CT to rule out cerebellar haemorrhage, which requires urgent neurosurgical care.

How does dysmetria help you differentiate a cerebellar stroke from a brainstem stroke? — Cerebellar lesions produce overshoot movements; brainstem strokes often cause cranial nerve deficits without dysmetria.

A patient with HIV on ART develops dysmetria; which opportunistic infection is most likely and what test confirms it? — Cerebral toxoplasmosis; MRI with contrast shows ring‑enhancing lesions, but if unavailable, start empirical therapy and monitor response.

Why is thiamine given before glucose in an alcoholic patient with dysmetria? — To prevent precipitating Wernicke’s encephalopathy; thiamine deficiency can coexist and glucose alone worsens neurologic injury.
What physiotherapy intervention is most beneficial after acute cerebellar infarct? — Coordination exercises focusing on proprioceptive feedback and balance training to improve functional mobility.

Explain why dysdiadochokinesia may accompany dysmetria and how you would test both at the bedside. — Both reflect cerebellar dysfunction; test rapid alternating hand movements for diadochokinesia and finger‑nose‑finger for dysmetria.

When is surgical decompression indicated in cerebellar swelling causing dysmetria? — When imaging shows mass effect with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus, and the patient deteriorates neurologically.

How would you manage dysmetria in a patient with chronic alcohol use where MRI is not available? — Perform CT to exclude bleed, give thiamine, advise abstinence, and arrange physiotherapy; treat any identified metabolic derangements.
ai.title: Dysmetria
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Dysmetria is a cerebellar coordination defect causing overshoot or undershoot of intended movements. It signals cerebellar pathology, often from vascular, infectious, or toxic causes, and guides focused neurological assessment.

b: Common sign in posterior‑fossa strokes, cerebellar tumours, chronic alcohol abuse, and infections (e.g., cerebral malaria, HIV‑related opportunistic infections).
Seen as ‘past pointing’ on the finger‑nose‑finger test.
sections.p: Dysmetria is the inability to judge distance or range of movement, leading to inaccurate reaching. It reflects dysfunction of the cerebellar hemispheres or deep nuclei.

b: Distinguish from dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements).
Severity graded by the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS) when available.
sections.p: The cerebellum fine‑tunes motor output; loss of this feedback produces dysmetria. It is a component of the broader ataxia spectrum.

b: Acute onset → think stroke, hemorrhage, or infection; urgent neuro‑imaging needed.
Sub‑acute/chronic → consider tumour, multiple sclerosis, alcohol, or drug toxicity.
sections.p: Identifying dysmetria directs the clinician to evaluate the posterior fossa and consider reversible causes.

t.b: Is there an acute bleed or infarct in the cerebellum? → Positive finding mandates neurosurgical review; negative does not rule out early ischemia.
Detects infarct, tumour, demyelination, or infection when CT is inconclusive. If MRI unavailable, rely on clinical picture and repeat CT.
Screen for infectious causes common in low‑resource settings. Positive malaria or HIV guides targeted therapy.

t.a: Serum electrolytes, liver function, vitamin B12
t.b: Identify metabolic/toxic contributors (e.g., hepatic encephalopathy, B12 deficiency). Treat underlying abnormality.

b: Acute cerebellar stroke – give antiplatelet (aspirin) unless contraindicated; manage intracranial pressure; arrange neurosurgical evaluation if edema threatens brainstem.
Infection (malaria, TB meningitis, HIV encephalitis) – start disease‑specific antimicrobial therapy; monitor for drug interactions with antiretrovirals.
Alcohol‑related cerebellar degeneration – abstinence, thiamine supplementation, physiotherapy.
Fall prevention – bedside rails, supervised ambulation, physiotherapy for coordination training.
sections.p: Treat the underlying aetiology, provide supportive care, and prevent complications such as falls.

b: Finger‑nose‑finger: overshoot = dysmetria; corrective attempts are jerky.
Heel‑shin test: lateral deviation indicates cerebellar involvement.
Rapid alternating movements (diadochokinesia) often impaired alongside dysmetria.
sections.p: Focus on bedside tests that reveal dysmetria and differentiate cerebellar lesions.

b: Attributing dysmetria to peripheral neuropathy – peripheral loss causes weakness, not overshoot.
Missing a treatable infection because imaging was unavailable – use bedside labs and empirical therapy when suspicion is high.
Neglecting fall risk – patients may suffer serious injuries without preventive measures.
sections.p: Pitfalls that lead to misdiagnosis or delayed care.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of coordination with headache, vomiting, or altered consciousness – possible cerebellar haemorrhage.
Progressive dysmetria with fever – consider meningitis or encephalitis.
